questions.question:
Consider the following given grammar: 
 
S -> Aa
A -> BD
B -> b| ε
D -> d| ε
Let a, b, d and $ be indexed as follows:

Compute the FOLLOW set of the non-terminal B and write the index values for the symbols in the FOLLOW set in the descending order. (For example, if the FOLLOW set is {a, b, d, $}, then the answer should be 3210).

questions.explanation:
A [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] BD, so B is followed by D: FOLLOW(B) gets FIRST(D) [latex]-[/latex] {[latex]\epsilon[/latex]} = {d}.
D can be [latex]\epsilon[/latex], so FOLLOW(B) also gets FOLLOW(A) = {a} (from S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Aa).

FOLLOW(B) = {a, d}. Indices: a = 3, d = 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] in descending order: 31.

Answer: 31

questions.question:
Consider the following three ANSI-C programs, [latex]\text{P1, P2,}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P3}[/latex].

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} \hline \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P1} & \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P2} & \quad\quad\quad \textbf{P3} \\ \hline \text{\#include < stdio.h >} & \text{\#include < stdio.h >} & \text{\#include < stdio.h >} \\ \begin{array}{l} \text{int a=5;} \\ \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=5;} \\ \quad \text{int a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} & \begin{array}{l} \text{int main()\{} \\ \quad \text{int a=5;} \\ \quad \text{float a=7;} \\ \quad \text{return(0);} \end{array} \\ {\text{\}}} & {\text{\}}} & {\text{\}}} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.A: Only [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] will compile without any error
options.B: Only [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] will compile without any error
options.C: Only [latex]\text{P3}[/latex] will compile without any error
options.D: All three programs [latex]\text{P1, P2,}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P3}[/latex] will compile without any error

questions.explanation:
P1: Global [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] and, inside [latex]\text{main()}[/latex], a separate local [latex]\text{int a=7;}[/latex]. This is perfectly legal C — the local declaration simply shadows the global one within [latex]\text{main}[/latex]'s scope. Compiles fine.

P2: [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] followed immediately by [latex]\text{int a=7;}[/latex] in the same block/scope — this is an illegal redeclaration of the same identifier [latex]a[/latex] within one scope, which is a compile-time error.

P3: [latex]\text{int a=5;}[/latex] followed by [latex]\text{float a=7;}[/latex] — again redeclaring [latex]a[/latex] in the same scope, this time with a conflicting type, which is also a compile-time error.

Answer: Only P1 will compile without any error.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects
options.B: The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth- first order
options.C: Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed
options.D: All  L-attributed  definitions  based  on  LR(1)  grammar  can  be  evaluated  using  a bottom-up parsing strategy

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- An attribute grammar is an SDD whose semantic rules have no side effects [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- "L-attributed definitions cannot always be evaluated in depth-first order" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. Every L-attributed definition can be evaluated by a left-to-right depth-first traversal; that is why they are called L-attributed.
- Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser during reductions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammars can be evaluated bottom-up" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. The marker non-terminal method is guaranteed only for L-attributed definitions on LL(1) grammars; adding markers can make an LR(1) grammar non-LR.

Answer: Options 2 and 4

Consider the basic block given below.

e =d - b

- n1 = b + c0 (a), n2 = n1 + d0 (c, e), n3 = b + n2 (d, a) (3 nodes, 2 edges each)

Answer: 6 and 6

questions.question:
Consider the following grammar [latex]G [/latex], with [latex]S [/latex] as the start symbol. The grammar [latex]G [/latex] has three incomplete productions denoted by (1), (2), and (3).

[latex] \begin{aligned} & S \rightarrow d a T \mid \quad(1) \\ & T \rightarrow a S|b T|(2) \\ & R \rightarrow \text { (3) } \mid \epsilon \end{aligned} [/latex]

The set of terminals is [latex]\{a, b, c, d, f\} [/latex]. The FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the different non-terminals are as follows.

[latex] \begin{aligned} & \operatorname{FIRST}(S)=\{c, d, f\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(T)=\{a, b, \epsilon\}, \operatorname{FIRST}(R)=\{c, \epsilon\} \\ & \operatorname{FOLLOW}(S)=\operatorname{FOLLOW}(T)=\{c, f, \$\}, \operatorname{FOLLOW}(R)=\{f\} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Which one of the following options CORRECTLY fills in the incomplete productions?

options.C:
(1) [latex]S \rightarrow f R [/latex]
(2) [latex]T \rightarrow c T [/latex]
(3) [latex]R \rightarrow c R [/latex]
options.D:
(1) [latex]S \rightarrow R f [/latex]
(2) [latex]T \rightarrow c T [/latex]
(3) [latex]R \rightarrow c R [/latex]

questions.explanation:
Use the given FIRST and FOLLOW sets:
- [latex]FIRST(S)=\{c,d,f\}[/latex] but [latex]daT[/latex] gives only d, so (1) must give c and f. [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex] gives [latex](FIRST(R)-\epsilon)\cup\{f\}=\{c,f\}[/latex] True ([latex]S\rightarrow fR[/latex] gives only f).
- [latex]\epsilon\in FIRST(T)[/latex], so (2) is [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex].
- [latex]FIRST(R)=\{c,\epsilon\}[/latex], so (3) starts with c.

Check FOLLOW with [latex]R\rightarrow cTR[/latex]: [latex]FOLLOW(T)\supseteq FIRST(R)-\epsilon=\{c\}[/latex] and [latex]FOLLOW(R)=\{f\}[/latex] (from [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex]); together with $ this gives [latex]FOLLOW(S)=FOLLOW(T)=\{c,f,\$\}[/latex] True. With [latex]R\rightarrow cR[/latex], c could never follow T.

Answer: (1) [latex]S\rightarrow Rf[/latex] (2) [latex]T\rightarrow\epsilon[/latex] (3) [latex]R\rightarrow cTR[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the syntax directed translation given by the following grammar and semantic rules. Here [latex]N, I, F \; and \; B[/latex] are non-terminals. [latex]N[/latex] is the starting non-terminal, and [latex]\#,0 \; and \; 1[/latex] are lexical tokens corresponding to input letters [latex]"\#","0" \; and \; "1"[/latex], respectively. [latex]X.val[/latex] denotes the synthesized attribute (a numeric value) associated with a non-terminal [latex]X[/latex]. [latex]I_1[/latex] and [latex]F_1[/latex] denote occurrences of [latex]I[/latex] and [latex]F[/latex] on the right hand side of a production, respectively. For the tokens [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex], [latex]0.val=0[/latex] and [latex]1.val=1[/latex].

The value computed by the translation scheme for the input string
[latex]\begin{aligned} N & \rightarrow I \# F & N.val=I.val+F.val \\ I &\rightarrow I_1B & I.val = (2 I1.val) + B.val\\ I &\rightarrow B&I.val = B.val\\ F &\rightarrow BF_1& F.val = \frac{1}{2}(B.val + F1.val)\\ F &\rightarrow B& F.val = \frac{1}{2} B.val\\ B&\rightarrow 0& B.val = 0.val\\ B &\rightarrow 1&B.val = 1.val \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]10\# 011[/latex]

is ____ (Rounded off to three decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Integer part "10" (binary):
I for "1" = 1; I for "10" = [latex]2\times1+0=2[/latex].

Fraction part "011" (evaluated right to left):
- F("1") = [latex]\frac12\times1=0.5[/latex]
- F("11") = [latex]\frac12(1+0.5)=0.75[/latex]
- F("011") = [latex]\frac12(0+0.75)=0.375[/latex]

N.val = 2 + 0.375 = 2.375 (i.e. binary 10.011).

Answer: 2.375

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

[latex]x[i]=(p+r)*(-s[i])+u/w[/latex], in evaluation order:

- (1) =[] s i [latex]\text{---}[/latex] fetch s[i]
- (2) uminus (1)
- (3) * (0) (2) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] (p+r) * ([latex]-[/latex]s[i])
- (4) / u w
- (5) + (3) (4)
- (6) []= x i [latex]\text{---}[/latex] location x[i] for storing
